title: Ajahn Funn: This being the case, it’s not really yours. It tends toward illness. When we’re born, we assume that we don’t already have any…
content:
Illnesses Filling the Body Down to Every Pore

This being the case, it’s not really yours. It tends toward illness. When we’re born, we assume that we don’t already have any illnesses. Doctors tell us that illnesses come from this or that thing outside, but the Buddha’s teachings tell us about the illnesses that already fill the body down to every pore.

Why do they say that? Cakkhu-rogo: The eye has its illnesses. Sota-rogo: The ear has its illnesses. There are diseases in the ear. Ghāna-rogo: illnesses in the nose. Jivhā-rogo: illnesses in the tongue. Kāya-rogo: illnesses in the body. Mano-rogo: illnesses in the heart—angina, tightness in the heart, the heart when it’s enlarged or its valves leak. Think about it. Hattha-rogo: illnesses in the hands. Pāda-rogo: illnesses in the feet. They run into this or that, get scrapes, get cut open and bleed. That’s an illness. Do you see? Kesa-rogo: illnesses in the hair on your head. It falls out or your scalp itches. Nakha-rogo: illnesses in the nails. Danta-rogo: illnesses in the teeth. They get eaten away with decay; they wiggle and get loose. Taca-rogo: illnesses in the skin. Every part of the body has its illnesses and malfunctions.

title: Ajahn Funn: Where do things get born? How do we get born in hell, born as common animals, born in suffering, born poor? Where does…
content:
What Falls into Hell, What Goes to Be a Deva or Brahmā: This Mind

Where do things get born? How do we get born in hell, born as common animals, born in suffering, born poor? Where does birth come from? It comes from this mind. What falls into hell, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into birth as a common animal? This mind. Mental happiness and mental ease are born from this mind. They’re not born from anything else. What goes to be a deva, an Indra, a Brahmā is this mind. Nothing else.

When this is the case, I want each of you to get your mind, your heart, quiet. So. Each and every one of you, make your heart quiet. I can promise you that whatever sound you may hear won’t pose you any danger. You don’t have to worry. Make your heart quiet. Make your heart still. Make your heart entirely empty. Don’t grasp onto this or that thing as your self. If you grasp, it’s suffering. Now’s the time to put the thread into the needle, so really focus on doing it.

title: Ajahn Funn: As long as birth after birth and death after death continue in this way, all the sufferings that arise dependent on birth, aging,…
content:
We Are Immersed in the Mass of Suffering – Strive Quickly on the Middle Way

As long as birth after birth and death after death continue in this way, all the sufferings that arise dependent on birth, aging, sickness, and death — called jātidukkhā (suffering of birth), jarādukkhā (suffering of aging), byādhidukkhā (suffering of sickness), maraṇadukkhā (suffering of death) — will keep tormenting beings in every realm and every existence, with no possibility of ending.

Therefore, when we see that birth, aging, sickness, and death exist within ourselves, that we ourselves are immersed in the mass of suffering dominated by birth, aging, sickness, and death — is it fitting that we remain deluded and negligent, not quickly striving on the path that leads away from suffering, the middle way (majjhimāpaṭipadā)? We should practice and follow it, and we should avoid the two extremes that monks should not pursue — love and hate — and instead dwell in seclusion (viveka): bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhiviveka). Let us all develop and cultivate these kinds of seclusion thoroughly, with skillful means and non-negligence (appamāda). Practicing in this way every day, at all times, we will have only happiness and peace, constantly and forever.

title: Ajahn Funn: Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho are our refuge. All of us here want to gain merit and wholesome qualities. Do you know merit yet? Have…
content:
Merit Is a Good Mind, Happy and at Ease, Cool-Hearted

Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho are our refuge. All of us here want to gain merit and wholesome qualities. Do you know merit yet? Have you gained merit? Do you see merit? Or don’t you know at all? You’ve come from far, far away, with great hardship and difficulty. If you don’t know merit, where will you get it? Does merit lie in this hall? In this forest? Haven’t you got it yet? It must be opanayiko – to be brought inside oneself, paccattaṃ – to be known personally. Merit is like this: the characteristic of merit is that our mind is good, our mind is happy, our mind is at ease, cool-hearted, free from suffering, heat, turmoil, and trouble. That is merit. Do you have it yet? Is your mind good yet? Look at your mind. If the mind is not good, how can you get merit? Is your mind good yet? Look. Look at your own mind. Alright, from now on listen to the Dhamma. Don’t just listen to the sound; listen to its source. Listen to the Dhamma.

title: Ajahn Funn: After consideration, he came to the conclusion that there must be something that doesn’t take birth, doesn’t age, doesn’t grow ill, doesn’t die.…
content:
The Buddha’s Three Knowledges: Past Lives, Passing Away and Arising, Ending of Defilements

After consideration, he came to the conclusion that there must be something that doesn’t take birth, doesn’t age, doesn’t grow ill, doesn’t die. Just as when there’s darkness, there’s light to relieve it; when there’s heat, there’s coolness to relieve it. He kept on exploring and contemplating for six years before he was able to achieve the unexcelled right self-awakening that made him a Buddha. His awakening consisted of three things:

Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa: He awakened to his past lives. What he had been born as, he knew it all, knew it thoroughly and throughout, with nothing concealed—whatever level of becoming he had taken birth in. This is why he knew all about living beings, because he had been everything that they were. Whoever had done what, he knew it all. This was the first knowledge.

Cutūpapāta-ñāṇa: the knowledge that allowed him to know how living beings, after falling away from this life, went to live on what level of becoming and birth, what they became: The Buddha knew it all. What they had done, what they had built up, that led them to be born on what level of becoming: He knew it all. He was capable and fearless after he had awakened to this.

Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa: This was the knowledge that ended becoming and birth—that made him an arahant. It disbanded defilement, passion, greed, aversion, delusion, ignorance, craving, clinging, becoming, and birth once and for all. He was never to swim around, dying and taking rebirth, ever again.

title: Ajahn Funn: When we do not commit those wrongs, then those wrongs do not exist. No one among us desires those five wrongs, no one…
content:
When We Do Not Commit the Five Wrongs, There Is No Offense

When we do not commit those wrongs, then those wrongs do not exist. No one among us desires those five wrongs, no one wants them. Let us all restrain and guard ourselves so that they do not arise within us. Those five are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, drinking alcohol and fermented liquor. If we do not do them, then there is no offense, no kamma, no sin, no evil. In whatever realm or birth we are born, we will be beautiful and handsome, with proper body, proper speech, proper mind. We will have happiness and ease. Why do we have happiness and ease? Because we have abandoned those five wrongs. Sīlena sugatiṃ yanti, sīlena bhogasampadā – by virtue one goes to a happy destiny, by virtue there is achievement of wealth. One has happiness and ease, one has material wealth and possessions, one is not suffering or poor. Why is one not suffering or poor? Because one is born complete. Our body is complete, our speech is complete, our mind is complete. Whatever we study, there is no obstruction; whatever work we do, there is no obstruction because there is no offense in us.

title: Ajahn Funn: So, what is the mind like? There is the mind of a villain, the mind of a prisoner. There is the mind that…
content:
The Mind Can Be Anything: Villain, Prisoner, Animal, Ghost, Indra, Brahmā

So, what is the mind like? There is the mind of a villain, the mind of a prisoner. There is the mind that is miserable and poor. There is the mind of an animal, the mind of a ghost or a hell-being. There is the mind of Indra or Brahmā, the mind of a great king or emperor, the mind of a wealthy millionaire, the mind of a beautiful person, a rich and fortunate person, someone who is neither poor nor suffering. There is the mind of a military officer, a general, a field marshal. The mind can be any of these. What can you say? Choose for yourself. You have come here – what do you want? The Dhamma is like this. The Buddha taught about our refuge. We have ordained, we have listened. In our ordination we received the precepts, and he told us what our refuge is. He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t say, “Possessions, money, and gold – saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” “Parents and siblings – saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” “Buildings and houses – saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” No one ever takes refuge in that way, right? There is only “Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi” – that’s it, isn’t it? Then “dutiyampi” – the second time, “tatiyampi” – the third time, “saraṇa-gamanaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ” – finished. This is our refuge. Apart from this, there is none.

title: Ajahn Funn: To move even closer in: “These eyes are mine, these ears are mine, this nose is mine, this tongue is mine, this body…
content:
If These Things Really Were Yours, Would You Have Them Go Bleary or Deaf?

To move even closer in: “These eyes are mine, these ears are mine, this nose is mine, this tongue is mine, this body is mine, this mind is mine”—but none of it’s true. How could it be yours? How can you depend on any of these things for long? You can’t even take your body with you. If these things really were yours, would you have your eyes go bleary? Would you have your ears go deaf? Your nose. Your body: Would you have it be in pain? Would you have it get too hot or too cold? If it really were yours, you wouldn’t do any of these things. So contemplate this. Don’t be deluded and infatuated. This body is the body of Māra—the Māras of the aggregates.

The Māras of the aggregates aren’t anything else: They’re form, feelings, perceptions, fabrications, consciousness. These are the Māras of the aggregates. Form is your body sitting right here. Feelings are feelings of pleasure or pain. Perceptions are labels and meanings. Fabrications are thoughts you put together. Consciousness is awareness. All of these things are Māras.

title: Ajahn Funn: Likewise, if our mind gets lost and turns toward attraction but doesn't get what it wants, we suffer. If it turns toward aversion,…
content:
Whatever Arises, Know It but Don't Cling – The Knower Is in the Middle of the Chest

Likewise, if our mind gets lost and turns toward attraction but doesn't get what it wants, we suffer. If it turns toward aversion, not wanting to see or hear something, but then sees or hears it anyway, we suffer, don't we? So we must not turn off. Walk the middle way. Whatever arises, know it, but don't cling to it.

Buddho, the knower, is right here in the middle of our chest. From now on, you should all come to know and see this. This is the practice, the conduct that reaches Dhamma, reaches Vinaya, reaches the religion. Know and reach your own body and mind. Right now, we don't reach our body. We don't reach our mind. Our mind floats off after sense objects: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects. It feeds on external objects. But when it reaches our body, it sees happiness and suffering. Why is there happiness? Because our mind is calm, still, equanimous – not sending itself forward, backward, left, right, up, or down. It stays fixed in the middle, right at that knowing. This mind is not something that is inherently suffering or difficult. It has been this way from the very beginning. But we mix all sorts of things into it, and so it becomes all sorts of things. Therefore, the Buddha taught us to let go.

title: Ajahn Funn: See? Sitting here, your mind is still suffering — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable. It torments body and self, pain here, ache there.…
content:
Kamma Arises from Body, Speech, and Heart – Mental Kamma Is the Inclining of Mind

See? Sitting here, your mind is still suffering — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable. It torments body and self, pain here, ache there. It gives rise to diseases, dangers, defilements, nuisances, evil and depravity, misery and hardship. This is vipassanā. We know clearly and see truly. The truths (sacca-dhamma) do not come from elsewhere. Quickly recollect Buddho to cut it off. Do not leave it. If we leave it, we will continue to be poor, suffering people, continue to be evil and depraved. We don't want these things, do we? So see: when the mind is not good, that is suffering. Contemplate until it is certain. This is what we call kamma — that or this. Where does kamma come from? Kamma does not come from the sky, air, trees, mountains, or hills. Kamma by body (kāya-kamma), kamma by speech (vacī-kamma), kamma by mind (mano-kamma) — kamma arises from our body, from our speech, from our heart.

So kamma arises from this. At this moment, our bodily kamma is already good, our verbal kamma is already gone. Only mental kamma remains — the inclining of mind. Whatever kamma we incline toward, whether good kamma or bad kamma. Kammassako mhi — I am the owner of my kamma.
